opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic motivation is that if you want a model of how AI automation affects the economy, you can't just assume a fixed path for how much people invest in compute, or in hardware R&D, or in training runs versus deployment. Those are choices that real actors make, and they respond to incentives. If AI is becoming dramatically more capable and the returns to investing in it are going up, you'd expect investment to respond to that. And conversely, if returns are low, people won't pour trillions of dollars into it.

So we wanted the investment decisions inside GATE to be endogenous. The natural way to do that in economics is to say there's some representative agent, or some planner, that's choosing how to allocate resources over time to maximize some objective, usually something like discounted utility of consumption. Then the allocation between, say, building more compute, doing more software research, or just consuming output falls out of that optimization rather than being something we hand-pick.

The advantage is that it gives you internal consistency. A lot of earlier forecasting work would take some trend, say compute spending growing at a certain rate, and extrapolate it. But that trend implicitly depends on what the economic returns are, and if your model says AI is going to automate a large fraction of tasks, then those returns change a lot, and the trend shouldn't be expected to hold. Optimization lets the model react to its own predictions, in a sense.

Now, I should say, it's obviously an idealization. Real-world actors aren't perfectly optimizing, they have uncertainty, there are coordination problems, there's regulation, and so on. So I wouldn't take the exact numbers from that part of the model too literally. But I think it's a much better baseline than assuming investment is fixed or just follows a historical trend, especially in a scenario where the economy might change very dramatically. And it helps you see the qualitative dynamic, which is that once AI starts being able to substitute for a lot of human labor, the incentive to scale up compute becomes enormous, and that feedback loop is really the core of why we think growth could accelerate.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes fixed investment assumptions and historical trends, but does not identify unreasonable behavior under extreme parameter values.

r002.rationale: It mentions uncertainty as a real-world complication, but does not explain that early investment can resolve uncertainty about full automation prospects.

r003.rationale: It describes optimization as internally consistent and useful for showing feedback dynamics, but does not present GATE as a way to expose incompatible beliefs about AI.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic reason is that if you don't have optimization, you don't really have a way of pinning down how the agents in the model respond to AI. You can write down a model where there's some exogenous rule, like "firms spend ten percent of their revenue on compute," or "when AI gets better, investment goes up by this much," but then all of the interesting dynamics are just being assumed by you. You're putting the answer in by hand. And the whole point of building GATE was that we didn't know the answer. We wanted the model to tell us something about how the economy would behave as AI gets more capable, and for that you need the agents to be responding to incentives in a way that's determined by the structure of the model rather than by us.

The way to think about it is that the economy is made up of people and firms that are trying to do well for themselves. When compute gets cheaper, or when AI systems can automate more tasks, that changes the returns to different kinds of investment, and people react to that. They shift spending toward compute, they build more fabs, they invest more in R&D, they substitute AI labor for human labor in the tasks where that's possible. Optimization is just the formal way of capturing "people respond to changing returns." If you don't have it, you have no principled way of saying how big those responses should be, and the responses are what drive the whole trajectory. The feedback loop where AI improves, that raises the return to investing in AI, which brings forward more investment, which improves AI further, that loop only exists if agents are actually choosing to invest based on the returns they expect.

There's also a more practical argument, which is that it imposes consistency. If you have a bunch of separate rules of thumb for how different parts of the economy behave, it's very easy to end up with something incoherent, where the implied behavior in one part of the model contradicts what's happening in another. When everything comes out of a single optimization problem, with agents who understand the production structure and the constraints, you're forced to be consistent, and that catches a lot of mistakes in your own thinking. Several times while building the model we had intuitions that turned out to be wrong once we worked out what an optimizing agent would actually do.

Now, I should be clear that this comes with costs. It's a lot harder to solve, especially with the kind of forward-looking behavior where agents anticipate future automation, and you have to make some simplifications that you might not love. Real people obviously aren't perfect optimizers with full knowledge of the production function. But I think the alternative, where you give up on optimization and just assume the behavior, is worse, because then the model isn't really telling you anything you didn't already put in. So we accepted the complexity in exchange for a model where the conclusions are actually a consequence of the assumptions about technology, rather than a restatement of assumptions about behavior.

r001.rationale: It criticizes hardcoded rules for assuming behavior and producing incoherent results, but does not mention unreasonable behavior at extreme parameter values.

r002.rationale: It discusses investment responding to returns, but not early investment resolving uncertainty about the prospects for full automation.

r003.rationale: It says optimization revealed mistaken intuitions and catches inconsistencies, but does not present GATE as a tool for exposing incompatible beliefs about AI.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that, as AI capabilities change, the economic decisions people make should change as well. How much should you invest in compute? How much should you spend on training a better model versus running the models you already have? Those decisions depend on the returns you expect, and those returns depend on what AI can do.

You could prescribe those choices directly—for example, assume that a fixed fraction of investment always goes into compute. But then you risk building your conclusions into those assumptions. We wanted those choices to emerge from the model, with actors allocating resources according to the benefits and costs they face.

That doesn’t mean we think everyone optimizes perfectly. It’s a simplifying assumption, but it gives us a consistent way to capture how economic behavior responds to technological change, rather than holding that behavior fixed as the technology changes.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed investment rules risk building conclusions into assumptions, but does not identify unreasonable behavior under extreme parameter values.

r002.rationale: It discusses investment choices and expected returns, but does not explain that early investment can resolve uncertainty about full automation.

r003.rationale: It presents GATE as modeling economic responses to technological change, but does not say it exposes incompatible beliefs about AI.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that economic decisions should respond to the circumstances in the model. If AI gets cheaper or more capable, firms should change how they produce things and where they invest. If you prescribe those decisions in advance, you risk building your conclusions into your assumptions.

Optimization gives us a consistent way to model those responses. You specify the available technologies, the constraints, and what people are trying to achieve, and then let the model work out the allocation of resources. That lets you capture tradeoffs—for example, between using compute for production today and investing in capabilities that could make production more efficient later.

Of course, that doesn’t mean real people solve these optimization problems perfectly. It’s a simplifying assumption, but it gives us a useful baseline for understanding which constraints matter and how decisions change when those constraints shift.

r001.rationale: The response says preset decisions can bake conclusions into assumptions, but it does not identify unreasonable behavior under extreme parameter values as a weakness.

r002.rationale: It mentions investing in capabilities to improve future production, but does not explain early investment as a way to resolve uncertainty about full automation.

r003.rationale: The response describes optimization as a modeling baseline, but does not present GATE as a tool for exposing incompatible beliefs about AI.
